references.text: Isaiah prophesies that the Lord will become a stumbling stone and a rock of offense to both houses of Israel. Jesus applies this concept to himself—blessed is the one who does not take offense at him.
Isaiah speaks of the cornerstone in Zion on whom one should believe and not be put to shame. The one who does not take offense at Jesus as this stone is blessed.
Those who wait for the Lord will not be put to shame. This parallels Jesus' words that blessed is the one who does not take offense—holding fast to faith without being disappointed.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says exactly the same thing to John's disciples: "Blessed is the one who does not take offense at me."
The people of Nazareth took offense at Jesus. This illustrates the opposite of the blessing Jesus gives in Luke 7:23—they were not blessed because they took offense.
Simeon prophesies that Jesus is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be spoken against. This points forward to the fact that many would take offense at him.
Paul quotes Isaiah about the stumbling stone in Zion and adds that whoever believes in him will not be put to shame—a direct parallel to Jesus' blessing on the one who does not take offense.

Peter quotes Isaiah about the cornerstone and the stumbling stone. For those who believe, the stone is precious, but for the unbelievers it is a stumbling stone and a rock of offense—linking back to Jesus' words about not taking offense.
Paul writes that the crucified Christ is an offense (skandalon) to Jews. The gospel message about Jesus became a stumbling block, and Jesus' blessing applies to those who nevertheless believe.
